lead: Observations never agree exactly. Some come from short levelling runs, some from long ones, some from angles turned many times. A weight is a number that says how much each observation deserves to be trusted. The most probable value makes the weighted sum of squared residuals least. This is least-squares adjustment, used in control networks, traverse closes and GNSS baselines. Only a few universities teach this chapter.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.2 for repeated angle observations, Chapter 4.6 for control runs, and Unit 1 for random and systematic error.

blocks.text: The true value is the exact number we cannot know. The observed value is what the instrument gives. Error = observed − true value; residual = observed − adjusted value. A weight w is a relative number: w = k/σ², where σ² is the error variance and k is any constant. A small variance gives a large weight.

For n equally precise observations of one quantity, their mean has weight n times one observation, and standard error σ/√n. A levelled height difference over a run of length L has weight proportional to 1/L, because random error grows as √L. A taped distance over length L also has weight proportional to 1/L. An angle turned n times has weight proportional to n. Weights may be scaled; only ratios matter. For a sum or difference, variances add; for a product of independent observations, the relative variances add: (σ<sub>xy</sub>/xy)² ≈ (σ<sub>x</sub>/x)² + (σ<sub>y</sub>/y)².
Choose the unknown x so that S = Σ wᵢ (lᵢ − x)² is least. Set dS/dx = 0. For direct observations of one quantity, the normal equation is x Σwᵢ = Σwᵢlᵢ, so x = Σwᵢlᵢ / Σwᵢ, the weighted mean.

For two unknowns x and y, write each observation as aᵢx + bᵢy = lᵢ. Minimising Σ wᵢ (aᵢx + bᵢy − lᵢ)² gives two normal equations: (Σw a²)x + (Σw ab)y = Σw a l and (Σw ab)x + (Σw b²)y = Σw b l. Solve them simultaneously.

After adjustment, vᵢ = lᵢ − adjusted value. With relative weights, σ₀ = √(Σw v²/(n−u)), where u is the number of unknowns. For a weighted mean u = 1, so the denominator is n−1; for two unknowns u = 2, so it is n−2. An observation of weight wᵢ has standard error σ₀/√wᵢ, and the weighted mean has σ₀/√Σw. Probable error PE = 0.6745σ. A residual larger than 3σ is doubtful; recheck it.

examples.question: The difference of level between two points is measured by three levelling runs: h₁ = 12.436 m over 2 km, h₂ = 12.448 m over 3 km and h₃ = 12.440 m over 5 km. Find the most probable difference of level.
steps: Scale by 30: w₁ = 15, w₂ = 10, w₃ = 6; Σw = 31.
Σwv² ≈ 0.000871 m², small; no run is rejected.
examples.answer: The most probable difference of level is 12.441 m.
examples.check:
w1, w2, w3 = 15, 10, 6
l1, l2, l3 = 12.436, 12.448, 12.440
sumw = w1 + w2 + w3
num = w1*l1 + w2*l2 + w3*l3
mean = num / sumw
v1, v2, v3 = l1 - mean, l2 - mean, l3 - mean
for value in (w1, w2, w3, sumw, num, mean, v1, v2, v3):
    print(f"{value:.3f}")

traps: Do not set w ∝ L for a levelling run. A long run has larger variance, so w ∝ 1/L.
Weight uses variance σ², not σ. Doubling σ quarters the weight.
Error is measured from the true value; residual is measured from the adjusted value. They are not the same.
Probable error is 0.6745σ, not σ; the 3σ rule uses the standard error.
In a weighted mean divide by Σw, not by the number of observations.

quiz.q: Define weight and give its formula.
quiz.a: w = k/σ²; k is a constant and σ² is the error variance. Larger weight means more trust.

quiz.q: Why does a 5 km levelling run have less weight than a 1 km run?
quiz.a: Random error grows as √L, so variance grows as L; hence w ∝ 1/L.

quiz.q: Observations 10.2, 10.3, 10.1 m have weights 3, 2, 1. Find the weighted mean.
A residual is 4.2σ. What do you do and why?
quiz.a: Recheck or reject it as doubtful; under normal errors a residual beyond 3σ is rare, so a mistake is likely.

quiz.q: A single angle has σ = 6″. Find σ of the mean of 9 repetitions and its weight relative to one observation.
quiz.a: σ_mean = 6/√9 = 2″; weight is 9 times one observation.
It minimises Σ w v², the weighted sum of squared residuals.

beyond: Not for the exam. Least-squares adjustment is the engine inside GNSS baseline processing, total-station network software and deformation monitoring. Modern work adds variance-covariance matrices and robust estimators for outliers. Search “observation equations”, “normal equations” and “least-squares adjustment”.
